title: Imbalanced Data

blocks.t: From the notes
Imbalanced data, as written

Imbalanced dataset — one class has far more rows than the other.
Example: fraud detection, where 99% of transactions are legitimate.

The problem: the model becomes biased towards the majority
class. Accuracy is misleading — predicting "not fraud" always gives
99% accuracy.
Solutions:

items:
Undersampling — remove rows from the majority class.
We lose data.

Oversampling — duplicate rows of the minority class.
Risk of overfitting.

SMOTE — Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique. Instead of
copying, it creates new synthetic points between a minority point and
its neighbours.

class_weight = 'balanced' — tell the algorithm to penalise
minority errors more.

blocks.t:
Use the right metric: precision, recall,
F1, ROC-AUC — not accuracy.

blocks.cap:
A 98:2 dataset. The middle panel is the accuracy paradox measured: a
model that predicts the majority class for everything scores 0.980 accuracy and
0.000 recall.

blocks.t: Metrics that survive imbalance
From the confusion matrix:

\text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad
\text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\qquad
F_1=\frac{2\cdot P\cdot R}{P+R},

F_\beta = (1+\beta^2)\frac{P\cdot R}{\beta^2 P + R}
\quad(\beta>1 \text{ weights recall}),

\text{TPR}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\qquad
\text{FPR}=\frac{FP}{FP+TN},\qquad
\text{Balanced accuracy}=\frac{\text{TPR}+\text{TNR}}{2}.
ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC — the one that matters

ROC-AUC is over-optimistic under heavy imbalance, and this is the
single most common mistake in the whole topic. The reason is in the
denominators:
\text{FPR}=\frac{FP}{FP+TN}.

When negatives vastly outnumber positives, $TN$ is enormous, so even thousands
of false positives barely move the FPR. The ROC curve hugs the corner and the
AUC looks excellent while the model is useless in practice.

Precision–Recall AUC (average precision) uses
$\text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}$, which has no $TN$ term at all. It is
therefore sensitive to exactly the errors that matter. Its random baseline is
the positive rate itself — so an AP of 0.30 on a 2% positive class is a
15$\times$ lift, whereas 0.30 on a balanced problem would be terrible.

blocks.cap:
The same two models, two curves. ROC-AUC is above 0.95 for both; the PR
curve shows what is actually happening. Right: sweeping the decision threshold
— the default 0.5 is far from optimal.

blocks.t: The resampling family

blocks.cap:
Six treatments of the same 94:6 dataset. Random oversampling stacks
duplicates on top of each other; SMOTE fills the convex hull of the minority
class; undersampling deletes most of the majority.

blocks.t:
SMOTE. For a minority point $x_i$, pick one of its $k$ minority nearest
neighbours $x_{nn}$ and create
x_{\text{new}} = x_i + \lambda (x_{nn} - x_i),\qquad \lambda\sim U(0,1).

The new point lies on the line segment between two real minority points. Because
it is a genuinely new location rather than a copy, the classifier's decision
region for the minority class expands rather than just becoming heavier
— which is the whole point.

head: Method
What it does
Notes
rows: Simple, no assumptions, but duplicates encourage memorisation. Surprisingly hard to beat.
Needs $\ge k+1$ minority rows; numeric features only; interpolates blindly into majority territory.
Concentrates effort where the decision actually happens.
More synthetic points where minority is hardest
Use these instead of SMOTE when categories exist.
Throws away information; fine when data is plentiful; very fast.
Removes majority points in boundary-crossing pairs
Keeps majority points nearest the minority
Usually the best of the resampling family.

blocks.t:
The single most dangerous mistake in this entire topic: resampling
before splitting. If you SMOTE the whole dataset and then split, a
synthetic point built from a training row can land in your test set — the test
set is contaminated with information derived from the training data, and your
score is a fiction.

Worse, it also breaks cross-validation. Resampling must happen inside
each fold, on the training portion only. This is precisely why
imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline exists: unlike sklearn's, it applies samplers
during fit and skips them during predict. Never call
fit_resample by hand outside a pipeline.

SMOTE breaks in high dimensions. Interpolation assumes the segment
between two minority neighbours lies in minority territory. In high dimensions,
neighbours are far apart (Topic 71), so the segment often cuts straight through
majority regions and manufactures label noise. On wide tabular data, class
weights usually beat SMOTE.

SMOTE also destroys calibration. You have changed the class prior, so
the predicted probabilities no longer reflect reality. If downstream code
consumes probabilities — expected-loss calculations, ranking by risk — either
correct the prior or skip resampling and use class_weight plus threshold
tuning instead.
What actually works

blocks.cap:
Six strategies on the same 98:2 problem, all evaluated correctly with
resampling inside the pipeline. Recall rises, precision falls, and average
precision — the ranking quality — barely changes.

blocks.t: The honest summary

Resampling and class weights mostly move the operating point, not the
model's ability to rank. That is why AP stays roughly flat while recall and
precision trade against each other.
So the recommended order is:

items:
Fix the metric first. PR-AUC or expected cost. Everything else is
guesswork until this is right.

Tune the threshold. Free, no retraining, no distortion of
probabilities, and usually the biggest single win. The default 0.5 is an
arbitrary convention, not a decision rule.

Try class_weight="balanced" (or
scale_pos_weight in XGBoost). One parameter, no data distortion,
keeps the pipeline simple.

Then try resampling, inside a pipeline, cross-validated —
RandomOverSampler first, then SMOTETomek.

Collect more minority data if at all possible. It beats every
algorithmic trick.

If the imbalance is extreme ($<0.1\%$), reframe as
anomaly detection: Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, or an autoencoder's
reconstruction error.

blocks.t: Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, StratifiedKFold,
                                     cross_val_score, GridSearchCV)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import (classification_report, confusion_matrix,
                             precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score,
                             roc_auc_score, f1_score, make_scorer, fbeta_score)
from imblearn.over_sampling import (SMOTE, RandomOverSampler, ADASYN,
                                    BorderlineSMOTE, SMOTENC)
from imblearn.under_sampling import RandomUnderSampler, TomekLinks
from imblearn.combine import SMOTETomek, SMOTEENN
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline          # <-- imblearn's, NOT sklearn's
from imblearn.ensemble import BalancedRandomForestClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20000, n_features=25, n_informative=10,
                           weights=[0.98, 0.02], flip_y=0.01, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                      stratify=y,        # ALWAYS stratify
                                      random_state=0)
print("train positives:", ytr.sum(), "of", len(ytr))

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE CORRECT PIPELINE -- sampler INSIDE, so it never touches validation
# ==================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scaler",  StandardScaler()),
    ("sampler", SMOTE(random_state=0, k_neighbors=5)),   # fit only, not predict
    ("clf",     LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
])

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
ap = cross_val_score(pipe, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=4)
print("CV average precision:", ap.round(4), "mean", round(ap.mean(), 4))

# THE WRONG WAY -- do not do this:
#   X_res, y_res = SMOTE().fit_resample(X, y)          # leaks into the test set
#   train_test_split(X_res, y_res)                     # score is meaningless
#
# Also wrong: sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline with a sampler -- it would try to
# resample at predict time too. imblearn's Pipeline skips samplers on predict.

# ==================================================================
# 2. THRESHOLD TUNING -- the cheapest and usually biggest win
# ==================================================================
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced")
clf.fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr)
proba = clf.predict_proba(StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xte))[:, 1]

prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(yte, proba)
f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-12)
best = thr[np.nanargmax(f1[:-1])]
print(f"default 0.5 -> F1 {f1_score(yte, (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)):.4f}")
print(f"tuned {best:.3f} -> F1 {f1_score(yte, (proba >= best).astype(int)):.4f}")

# If you know the costs, optimise EXPECTED COST instead of F1 -- this is the
# only truly principled threshold.
COST_FN, COST_FP = 500.0, 10.0        # e.g. rupees per missed fraud / false alarm
costs = [((yte == 1) & (proba < t)).sum() * COST_FN +
         ((yte == 0) & (proba >= t)).sum() * COST_FP
         for t in np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99)]
t_star = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99)[int(np.argmin(costs))]
print(f"cost-optimal threshold {t_star:.2f}, cost {min(costs):,.0f}")

# ==================================================================
# 3. CLASS WEIGHTS -- one parameter, no data distortion
# ==================================================================
for cw in (None, "balanced", {0: 1, 1: 30}):
    m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight=cw)
    s = cross_val_score(m, StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr,
                        cv=cv, scoring="average_precision").mean()
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):14s} AP={s:.4f}")

# "balanced" sets w_k = n / (n_classes * n_k) -- inversely proportional to
# frequency. Tree ensembles have it too; XGBoost uses scale_pos_weight.

# ==================================================================
# 4. COMPARING SAMPLERS PROPERLY
# ==================================================================
samplers = {
    "none":              None,
    "RandomOverSampler": RandomOverSampler(random_state=0),
    "SMOTE":             SMOTE(random_state=0),
    "BorderlineSMOTE":   BorderlineSMOTE(random_state=0),
    "ADASYN":            ADASYN(random_state=0),
    "RandomUnder":       RandomUnderSampler(random_state=0),
    "SMOTETomek":        SMOTETomek(random_state=0),
}
for name, s in samplers.items():
    steps = [("sc", StandardScaler())]
    if s is not None:
        steps.append(("samp", s))
    steps.append(("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)))
    score = cross_val_score(Pipeline(steps), Xtr, ytr, cv=cv,
                            scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=4).mean()
    print(f"{name:18s} AP={score:.4f}")

# sampling_strategy controls HOW balanced -- full 1:1 is rarely optimal.
partial = SMOTE(sampling_strategy=0.3, random_state=0)   # minority -> 30% of majority

# ==================================================================
# 5. CATEGORICAL FEATURES -- plain SMOTE is WRONG
# ==================================================================
# SMOTE interpolates: the average of "Delhi" and "Mumbai" is meaningless.
# SMOTENC handles mixed data; SMOTEN handles all-categorical.
#   sm = SMOTENC(categorical_features=[3, 7, 11], random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 6. ENSEMBLES BUILT FOR IMBALANCE
# ==================================================================
brf = BalancedRandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0,
                                     sampling_strategy="all",
                                     replacement=True, n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("BalancedRF AP:", round(average_precision_score(
      yte, brf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))
# Each tree is grown on a balanced bootstrap -- no data is permanently lost,
# because different trees see different majority subsets.

# XGBoost's built-in handling:
#   scale_pos_weight = (y == 0).sum() / (y == 1).sum()

# ==================================================================
# 7. TUNING WITH THE RIGHT SCORER
# ==================================================================
f2 = make_scorer(fbeta_score, beta=2)      # beta > 1 weights RECALL higher
gs = GridSearchCV(
        Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()),
                  ("samp", SMOTE(random_state=0)),
                  ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=4))]),
        {"samp__sampling_strategy": [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0],
         "samp__k_neighbors":       [3, 5],
         "clf__n_estimators":       [200],
         "clf__max_depth":          [None, 12]},
        cv=cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("best:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# ==================================================================
# 8. EXTREME IMBALANCE (<0.1%) -- stop classifying, start detecting
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=0).fit(Xtr[ytr == 0])
scores = -iso.score_samples(Xte)          # higher = more anomalous
print("IsolationForest AP:", round(average_precision_score(yte, scores), 4))
# Trained on the majority class ONLY -- it never needs a labelled positive.
Everything on one page
Summary

The problem: accuracy is dominated by the majority class, so a
do-nothing model looks excellent. Never report accuracy on imbalanced data.

Metrics: PR-AUC / average precision is the default for rare positives,
because precision has no $TN$ term. ROC-AUC is inflated by the huge $TN$ count.
Best of all is expected cost, when the costs are known.

Threshold: 0.5 is a convention, not a decision. Tune it on validation
data — free, no retraining, and usually the biggest win.

Class weights: class_weight="balanced" sets
$w_k=\frac{n}{K n_k}$; scale_pos_weight in XGBoost. One parameter, no
distortion of the data.

Resampling: SMOTE creates $x_{new}=x_i+\lambda(x_{nn}-x_i)$ along
minority kNN segments. Variants: Borderline (near the boundary), ADASYN
(adaptive), SMOTENC (mixed types), SMOTETomek (oversample then clean).

The cardinal rule: resample inside the pipeline, inside each
CV fold, on training data only. Use imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline, and
always stratify your splits.

Reality check: resampling mostly relocates the operating point rather
than improving ranking. Fix the metric, tune the threshold, add class weights,
and only then reach for SMOTE.
Extreme imbalance ($<$0.1%): treat it as anomaly detection instead.
Interview corner
Q. Why is accuracy the wrong metric here?

Because predicting the majority class for everything achieves the majority
class's frequency as accuracy — 99% on a 1% positive problem — while
finding nothing. Accuracy is dominated by the $TN$ cell, which is exactly the
cell nobody cares about.
Q. ROC-AUC or PR-AUC?

PR-AUC when positives are rare. FPR $=FP/(FP+TN)$ has an enormous denominator
under imbalance, so thousands of false positives barely move the ROC curve.
Precision $=TP/(TP+FP)$ contains no $TN$ term and reflects the alerts a human
would actually have to triage.
Q. How does SMOTE work, and when does it fail?

It picks a minority point, picks one of its $k$ minority nearest neighbours, and
places a synthetic point randomly along the segment between them. It fails in
high dimensions (the segment crosses majority territory), with categorical
features (interpolation is meaningless — use SMOTENC), when the minority class
is very small (fewer than $k+1$ points), and when minority points are noise
(it amplifies them).
Q. Where exactly must resampling happen?

Inside the pipeline, on the training fold only. Resampling before the split
leaks synthetic points derived from training rows into the test set. Use
imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline, which applies samplers during fit and
skips them during predict.
Q. Oversampling or undersampling?

Oversampling when data is scarce — you cannot afford to discard majority rows.
Undersampling when data is plentiful and training cost matters; it is also much
faster. Combined approaches (SMOTETomek, SMOTEENN) usually beat either alone,
and BalancedRandomForest gets undersampling's speed without permanently
discarding anything.
Q. What does class_weight="balanced" do?

Sets $w_k = \frac{n}{K\,n_k}$, so each class contributes equally to the total
loss. It is mathematically similar to oversampling by duplication, but it
changes the loss rather than the data — no memory overhead and no synthetic
points.
Q. Is 0.5 ever the right threshold?

Only by coincidence. It is optimal for accuracy on a balanced problem with equal
error costs. Under imbalance or asymmetric costs the optimal threshold is
$\frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP}+C_{FN}}$ for a calibrated model — often far below 0.5.
Q. Does resampling change your probability estimates?

Yes — it changes the class prior, so predicted probabilities are inflated for
the minority class and no longer calibrated. If probabilities matter downstream,
either correct for the prior shift, or avoid resampling and use class weights
with threshold tuning.
Q. When would you not treat it as a classification problem at all?

When the positive rate is below roughly 0.1%, or when positives are so
heterogeneous that "positive" is not really one class. Then use anomaly
detection — Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, autoencoder reconstruction error
— which trains on the majority class alone and needs no labelled positives.

Q. Your model has 0.99 ROC-AUC but the business says it is useless.
What happened?

Almost certainly precision. At the operating threshold the alert list is
dominated by false positives, because a tiny FPR times an enormous negative
count is still a large absolute number. Look at the PR curve, compute precision
at the actual alert volume the team can handle (precision@k), and tune the
threshold against expected cost rather than F1.
Worked Examples
Four ways to rebalance 50 spam in 1000 emails
Start: 1000 emails, 50 spam (5%), 950 legitimate.
Baseline – always predict legitimate. Accuracy $=950/1000 = 95\%$, spam recall $=0$. High accuracy, zero usefulness.
Undersampling. Keep all 50 spam, randomly keep 50 legitimate, discard 900. Result: 100 rows, 50/50. Cheap, but throws away 900 real examples of legitimate mail.
Random oversampling. Keep all 950 legitimate, duplicate spam rows until it reaches 950: 1900 rows. No information lost, but the model can memorise the 50 originals many times, so it overfits them.
SMOTE. Pick a spam point $x_i = (2,4)$ and a spam neighbour $x_{nn} = (4,8)$. Create a synthetic point $x_{\text{new}} = x_i + \lambda(x_{nn}-x_i)$ with $\lambda \in [0,1]$. For $\lambda = 0.4$:
A new spam point on the line segment, not a copy. Apply to the minority class only, and fit SMOTE inside each cross-validation fold, never before the split.
Class weights (cost-sensitive). Balanced weights: $w_c = \dfrac{n}{k\cdot n_c}$, here $k=2$:
w_{\text{spam}} = \frac{1000}{2\cdot 50} = 10, \qquad w_{\text{legit}} = \frac{1000}{2\cdot 950} = 0.526
One spam error now costs as much as 19 legitimate errors. No data changes; the loss does.
Which to use. Start with class weights (no data change). Add SMOTE or resampling if the model still under-learns the minority. Always evaluate with precision, recall and PR-AUC, never accuracy.
